S01-01.method: solve the two equations of motion and eliminate a
S01-01.working: 2mg - T = 2ma and T - mg = ma; adding gives mg = 3ma so a = g/3; T = m(g + a) = m(g + g/3) = 4mg/3

S01-02.method: reduce the parallel pair, then divide the supply

S01-03.method: balance weight against drag by dimensions
S01-03.working: weight ~ rho_w g r^3 and drag ~ rho_air r^2 v^2; equating them cancels r^2 and one r, leaving v^2 ~ r, so v ~ sqrt(r)

S01-04.method: momentum first, then energy in the spring

S01-05.method: differentiate P(R) and set to zero
S01-05.working: P = E^2 R/(R + r)^2; dP/dR = 0 at R = r; then P = E^2 r/(2r)^2 = E^2/(4r)

S01-06.method: turn a pressure into a mass through g
S01-06.working: p = 1.0e5 Pa is a weight per square metre, so W = 1.0e5 N on 1 m^2; m = W/g = 1.0e5/10 = 1.0e4 kg

S01-07.method: find the speed at h, then double the time to the apex
S01-07.working: v^2 = u^2 - 2gh at height h; time from h up to the apex is v/g and the return takes the same, so the interval is 2v/g = 2sqrt(u^2 - 2gh)/g

S01-08.working: weight 20 x 10 = 200 N at 2.0 m; the perpendicular component of T at 4.0 m is T sin30 = T/2; 200 x 2.0 = (T/2) x 4.0 gives 400 = 2T so T = 200 N

S01-09.method: set the contact force to zero at the top
S01-09.working: mg - N = mv^2/r and the car leaves when N = 0, so v^2 = rg = 20 x 10 = 200; v = 14.1 m/s, so it leaves above about 14 m/s

S01-10.method: recognise an odd-harmonic series and find its step
S01-10.working: a pipe closed at one end gives only odd multiples of f0; the three given frequencies differ by 200 Hz, and 100, 300, 500, 700 are the odd multiples 1, 3, 5, 7 of 100 Hz, so f0 = 100 Hz

S01-11.method: put the critical angle equal to the fixed 45 degrees
S01-11.working: TIR needs theta > theta_c with sin(theta_c) = 1/n; the geometry fixes theta = 45, so the smallest n is the equality case 1/sin45 = 1/(1/sqrt2) = sqrt2

S01-12.method: reduce each configuration to one resistance, then divide the two terminal p.d.s
S01-12.working: before: 6.0 || 3.0 = 18/9 = 2.0 ohm so R_ext = 6.0 + 2.0 = 8.0 ohm; I = 12/(8.0 + 1.0) = 4/3 A and V = (4/3)(8.0) = 32/3 V.  after removing the 3.0 ohm: R_ext = 6.0 + 6.0 = 12.0 ohm, I = 12/13 A, V = (12/13)(12) = 144/13 V.  ratio = (144/13)/(32/3) = 432/416 = 27/26, and 27/26 is greater than 1 as it must be, since the load got lighter

S01-13.method: set heat lost equal to heat gained

S01-14.method: share the energy in inverse proportion to mass
S01-14.working: equal and opposite momenta, so KE = p^2/2m means KE goes as 1/m; the alpha has mass number 4 and the recoil A - 4, so the alpha takes (A-4)/((A-4)+4) = (A-4)/A of E

S01-15.method: substitute the constant-volume area into R = rho L / A
S01-15.working: volume fixed means A -> A/(1 + x); R' = rho L(1 + x)/(A/(1 + x)) = R(1 + x)^2; the fractional change is 2x + x^2, which for small x is 2x

S01-16.method: one position equation for the whole flight, then the positive root of the quadratic
S01-16.working: take up as positive with the origin at the release point: y = u t - g t^2/2.  Landing is y = -h, so g t^2/2 - u t - h = 0 and t = (u + sqrt(u^2 + 2gh))/g, the positive root (the other is a time before the throw).  Check with u = 10, g = 10, h = 120: sqrt(100 + 2400) = 50 so t = 60/10 = 6.0 s, and y = 10(6) - 5(36) = -120 m, which is the foot of the cliff

S01-17.method: add the gravity component and limiting friction, then equate to mg
S01-17.working: down the slope: mg sin(theta) = 5.0 x 10 x 0.60 = 30 N; normal reaction 5.0 x 10 x 0.80 = 40 N so limiting friction 0.50 x 40 = 20 N; needed pull 30 + 20 = 50 N; the hanging weight is 10m, so m = 5.0 kg

S01-18.method: require the centripetal acceleration to be g, then convert to a period
S01-18.working: omega^2 r = g so omega^2 = 10/50 = 0.20 and omega = 0.447 rad/s; T = 2 pi/omega = 6.283/0.447 = 14.1 s; equivalently T = 2 pi sqrt(r/g) = 2 pi sqrt5 = 14.1 s

S01-19.method: take the area of the triangle under the straight region
S01-19.working: energy per unit volume = (1/2) x stress x strain = 0.5 x 3.0e8 x 1.5e-3 = 0.5 x 4.5e5 = 2.25e5, which is 2.3e5 J/m^3 to two figures

S01-20.method: use sin(theta) <= 1 and round the inequality down
S01-20.working: d = 1e-3/500 = 2.0e-6 m and lambda = 6.0e-7 m; d/lambda = 2.0e-6/6.0e-7 = 3.33; n <= 3.33 so the highest order is 3; the fourth would need sin(theta) = 4 x 0.30 = 1.20, which does not exist

S01-21.method: combine the critical angle with Snell's law at the end face
S01-21.working: sin(theta_c) = 1.2/1.5 = 0.8; the steepest guided ray makes 90 - theta_c with the axis, so sin(alpha) = cos(theta_c) = sqrt(1 - 0.64) = 0.6; Snell gives sin(theta_a) = 1.5 x 0.6 = 0.9, which is also sqrt(1.5^2 - 1.2^2) = sqrt0.81

S01-23.method: conserve charge over the new total capacitance
S01-23.working: Q = CV = 2.0e-6 x 100 = 2.0e-4 C; the charge is shared over 2.0 + 3.0 = 5.0 uF; V = 2.0e-4/5.0e-6 = 40 V

S01-24.method: add the water pressure to the atmosphere, then use Boyle's law
S01-24.working: p_bottom = 1.0e5 + 1000 x 10 x 20 = 1.0e5 + 2.0e5 = 3.0e5 Pa; isothermal, so p1 V1 = p2 V2 gives 3.0e5 x 1.0 = 1.0e5 x V2 and V2 = 3.0 cm^3

S01-25.method: raise one half to the power of the number of half-lives

S02-01.method: match dimensions and take the square root
S02-01.working: [v] = L T^-1; [gamma] = N/m = M T^-2; [rho] = M L^-3; [lambda] = L. Try gamma/(rho lambda): (M T^-2)/((M L^-3)(L)) = (M T^-2)/(M L^-2) = L^2 T^-2; square root gives L T^-1, which is a speed. The other four: sqrt(gamma rho/lambda) = M L^-2 T^-1; sqrt(gamma lambda/rho) = L^2 T^-1; gamma/(rho lambda) = L^2 T^-2; sqrt(gamma rho)/lambda = M L^-5/2 T^-1

S02-02.method: write the self-similar relation and solve the quadratic
S02-02.working: R_eq = R + R R_eq/(R + R_eq); multiply out: R_eq^2 = R^2 + R R_eq; R_eq^2 - R R_eq - R^2 = 0; R_eq = R(1 + sqrt5)/2. Numerical check with R = 1: 1 + 1.618/2.618 = 1 + 0.618 = 1.618, which is the root

S02-03.method: photon energy first, then compare with EACH work function before subtracting
S02-03.working: hc = 1240 eV nm, so at 400 nm the photon energy is 1240/400 = 3.1 eV.  Metal A: 3.1 > 2.0 so it emits, and KE_max = 3.1 - 2.0 = 1.1 eV, so the stopping potential is 1.1 V.  Metal B: 3.1 < 3.5 so nothing is emitted; B's threshold is 1240/3.5 = 354 nm and 400 nm is longer than that

S02-04.method: build the series and sum it
S02-04.working: t_0 = sqrt(2h/g). Rebound to h/4 gives a rise-and-fall of 2 sqrt(2(h/4)/g) = 2 x (1/2) sqrt(2h/g) = t_0, so the bounces are t_0, t_0/2, t_0/4, ... Total = t_0 + t_0(1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + ...) = t_0 + t_0 x 2 = 3 sqrt(2h/g)

S02-05.method: divide the two force equations to kill the tension
S02-05.working: T cos(theta) = mg and T sin(theta) = m omega^2 L sin(theta) so T = m omega^2 L; dividing gives 1/cos(theta) = omega^2 L/g, so omega^2 = g/(L cos theta) and T = 2 pi sqrt(L cos theta/g)

S02-06.working: mass arriving per second = rho A v; it carries speed v and leaves with none, so the momentum destroyed per second is (rho A v)(v) = rho A v^2, and that is the force. Units: (kg m^-3)(m^2)(m^2 s^-2) = kg m s^-2 = N

S02-07.method: write the extension for each wire and equate
S02-07.working: e = FL/(AE) for the first. For the second A falls by a factor of four (diameter halved) and L doubles, so e = F2(2L)/((A/4)E) = 8 F2 L/(AE). Equating: F L/(AE) = 8 F2 L/(AE) so F2 = F/8

S02-08.method: approaching source, so the denominator is v minus the source speed

S02-09.method: apply the minimum-deviation relation and undo the sine
S02-09.working: n sin(A/2) = sin((A + D)/2) with A = 60 and n = sqrt2: sqrt2 x sin30 = sqrt2 x 0.5 = 0.7071 = sin45, so (60 + D)/2 = 45 and D = 30 deg

S02-10.method: common voltage, so power goes as 1/R
S02-10.working: P_3 = V^2/3 and P_6 = V^2/6, total = V^2(2/6 + 1/6) = V^2/2. Fraction = (V^2/3)/(V^2/2) = 2/3, and the smaller resistor takes the larger share

S02-11.method: count the halvings on a logarithmic axis
S02-11.working: 800/100 = 8 and 8 = 2^3, so three halvings span the twelve minutes; T = 12/3 = 4 min. Check: 800 -> 400 -> 200 -> 100 lands on the stated point

S02-12.method: reduce from the inside out, keeping the internal resistance in the loop
S02-12.working: 6 || 6 = 3; R_ext = 3 + 3 = 6; R_total = 6 + 2 = 8; I = 12/8 = 1.5 A; P = I^2 R = 2.25 x 3 = 6.75 W. Check: terminal p.d. 12 - 3 = 9 V, drop across the 3 ohm is 4.5 V, leaving 4.5 V across the pair, which 1.5 A gives

S02-13.method: momentum through the embedding, then friction doing work to the stop
S02-13.working: p = 20 x 300 = 6000 g m/s shared by 2000 g, so V = 3.0 m/s.  KE after = (1/2)(2.00)(3.0^2) = 9.0 J.  Friction force = mu x 2.00 x 10 = 20 mu, work over 1.5 m = 30 mu, so 30 mu = 9.0 and mu = 0.30.  Cross-check: KE before was 900 J, so 99% went in the embedding

S02-14.method: conserve charge, then compare the two energies
S02-14.working: Q = CV is fixed. C_total = C + 2C = 3C so V_new = Q/(3C) = V/3. E_before = Q^2/(2C); E_after = Q^2/(6C). Ratio 1/3 remains, so 2/3 is lost. Check: the result contains no resistance, so a thicker wire loses the same 2/3

S02-15.method: floating means submerged fraction equals the density ratio
S02-15.working: rho_L V_sub g = rho_b V g so V_sub/V = rho_b/rho_L. Water: 3/4 = rho_b/1000 so rho_b = 750. Unknown liquid: 1/2 = 750/rho_L so rho_L = 1500 kg/m^3. Direction: denser liquid holds the block higher, and 1/2 < 3/4

S02-16.method: longest wavelength that still gives a minimum
S02-16.working: delta = 3.5 - 2.5 = 1.0 m. Minimum needs delta = (n + 1/2)lambda, so the longest wavelength is at n = 0: lambda = 2 x 1.0 = 2.0 m. f = 340/2.0 = 170 Hz. Next member: lambda = 1.0/1.5 = 0.67 m giving 510 Hz, so 170 Hz is the lowest

S02-17.method: gradient gives stiffness, then convert to the modulus

S02-18.method: reduce to a proportionality before putting anything in
S02-18.working: E = hc/lambda and N = P/E, so N = P lambda/(hc) and N is proportional to P lambda. Doubling P doubles N; halving lambda halves N; the product of the two factors is 2 x 1/2 = 1, so N is unchanged

S02-19.method: divide by the large quantity, then expand
S02-19.working: kK/(k + K); divide top and bottom by K: k/(1 + k/K). With x = k/K small and n = -1, (1 + x)^n = 1 + nx gives 1 - k/K, so the result is k(1 - k/K). Numerical check with k = 1, K = 100: 100/101 = 0.990099 and 1 - 0.01 = 0.99

S02-20.method: count the positions in the ring, then remove the object
S02-20.working: Repeated reflection in two planes meeting at 60 deg is rotation in steps of 60 deg, so the bead and its images occupy 360/60 = 6 equally spaced positions. One of those is the bead, so the number of images is 6 - 1 = 5

S02-21.working: Every pair of levels gives a possible photon energy, because a single gamma can carry the whole difference. With four levels: 3 + 2 + 1 = 6. The six differences are 7, 6, 4, 3, 2 and 1 MeV, all distinct

S02-22.working: v_1 - v_2 = g(t + delta_t) - g t = g delta_t, a constant. Separation = (1/2)g(t + delta_t)^2 - (1/2)g t^2 = g delta_t t + (1/2)g delta_t^2, which is linear in t. So it grows at a constant rate. At t = 0 it is already (1/2)g delta_t^2, the head start

S02-23.method: pressure balance at the lower mercury surface
S02-23.working: rho_oil h = rho_Hg (2x), so x = rho_oil h/(2 rho_Hg). In centimetres: 850 x 16/(2 x 13600) = 13600/27200 = 0.5 cm = 5.0 mm. Check the size: 0.5/16 = 1/32, and the densities are in the ratio 13600/850 = 16

S02-24.method: density times volume, then check against a known mass
S02-24.working: V = 10 x 8 x 3 = 240 m^3; m = 1.2 x 240 = 288 kg, about 300 kg. Check: the same room full of water would be 240 x 1000 = 240000 kg, and air is about a thousandth as dense, so a few hundred kilograms is right

S02-25.method: find the photon energy, double it, subtract the same work function
S02-25.working: hf = phi + E_k = 2.0 + 1.0 = 3.0 eV. Halving lambda doubles hf to 6.0 eV. The work function is a property of the metal, so E_k = 6.0 - 2.0 = 4.0 eV. Check the direction: the photon energy doubled but the kinetic energy went up by four, which is what a fixed subtraction does

S03-01.method: take moments about B, so the unknown there drops out
S03-01.working: uniform beam: the 240 N acts at the 3.0 m midpoint. The load is 2.0 m from A, so 6.0 - 2.0 = 4.0 m from B. F_A x 6.0 = 240 x 3.0 + 360 x 4.0 = 720 + 1440 = 2160; F_A = 2160/6.0 = 360 N. Check: the two supports carry 600 N, so B has 240 N, and moments about A give F_B x 6.0 = 240 x 3.0 + 360 x 2.0 = 1440, F_B = 240 N

S03-02.method: put each candidate through the base dimensions
S03-02.working: [gamma] = N/m = kg s^-2; [rho] = kg m^-3; [r] = m; want s^-1. gamma/(rho r^3) = (kg s^-2)/((kg m^-3)(m^3)) = (kg s^-2)/kg = s^-2, and the square root is s^-1, a frequency. Rejected: gamma/(rho r) gives m^2 s^-2, whose root is m s^-1, a speed; gamma r^3/rho gives m^6 s^-2; gamma rho/r^3 gives kg^2 m^-6 s^-2; and gamma/(rho r^3) without the root is a frequency squared

S03-03.method: set limiting friction equal to the weight
S03-03.working: the wall pushes back horizontally with the whole push, so N = F and the limiting friction is mu N = 0.40 F. On the point of sliding down, 0.40 F = mg = 2.0 x 10 = 20 N, so F = 20/0.40 = 50 N. Check: F = 50 N gives N = 50 N and f_max = 20 N, exactly the weight, so the block is on the point of moving and no smaller push holds

S03-04.method: balance is a ratio between the two dividers
S03-04.working: balance needs the detector nodes at the same potential: 3.0/3.0 = 6.0/R, so R = 6.0 k. Check by potentials: the top node sits at 12 x 6.0/(3.0 + 6.0) = 8.0 V and the bottom node at 12 x 6.0/(3.0 + 6.0) = 8.0 V, equal, so no current flows through G

S03-05.method: turn the gradient into a rate of climb
S03-05.working: a 10% gradient means tan(theta) = 0.10, and at that small angle sin(theta) is also about 0.10. Rising at 5.0 x 0.10 = 0.50 m/s against a weight of 80 x 10 = 800 N needs 800 x 0.50 = 400 W. Check the size: lifting 800 N half a metre every second is 400 J per second

S03-06.method: stage the journey, then divide the whole distance by the whole time

S03-07.method: use the elastic result for a stationary target
S03-07.working: v_target = 2 m u/(m + 3m) = 2mu/(4m) = u/2. Check against both conservation laws: the incoming particle keeps (m - 3m)/(4m) u = -u/2, so p_after = m(-u/2) + 3m(u/2) = mu = p_before; and KE after = (1/2)m(u/2)^2 + (1/2)(3m)(u/2)^2 = mu^2/8 + 3mu^2/8 = mu^2/2 = KE before

S03-08.method: count three loops, so the length holds three half wavelengths
S03-08.working: the third harmonic has three loops, so L = 3 lambda/2 and lambda = 2L/3 = 2(0.60)/3 = 0.40 m. f = v/lambda = 120/0.40 = 300 Hz. Check: the fundamental is v/2L = 120/1.2 = 100 Hz and the third harmonic is 3 x 100 = 300 Hz

S03-09.method: divide the real depth by the refractive index
S03-09.working: for near-normal viewing the apparent depth is real depth / n = 2.4/1.5 = 1.6 m. Check the direction: a ray leaving the water bends away from the normal, so the stone is seen higher than it is, and 1.6 is less than 2.4

S03-10.method: reduce the loaded pair, then divide the supply
S03-10.working: the load puts 3.0 k in parallel with 3.0 k: (3.0 x 3.0)/(3.0 + 3.0) = 1.5 k. Total 6.0 + 1.5 = 7.5 k, so the parallel section takes 12 x 1.5/7.5 = 2.4 V. Check against the unloaded divider: without the load the tap gives 12 x 3.0/9.0 = 4.0 V, and loading a divider can only pull the tap down, so 2.4 is less than 4.0

S03-11.method: compare the heat available with the heat needed before assuming anything melts
S03-11.working: warm the ice to 0 C: 0.20 x 2100 x 10 = 4200 J.  melt it all: 0.20 x 3.3e5 = 66000 J, so 70200 J is needed.  the water can give at most 0.40 x 4200 x 30 = 50400 J, which is not enough, so ice survives at 0 C.  heat left for melting = 50400 - 4200 = 46200 J, so 46200/3.3e5 = 0.14 kg melts and 0.20 - 0.14 = 0.060 kg remains

S03-12.method: show that volume and mass both go as A
S03-12.working: V = (4/3) pi r^3 = (4/3) pi r0^3 A, so the volume is proportional to A, and the mass is proportional to A as well. Density = mass/volume is therefore independent of A, so it is unchanged. Check with the two values: A = 27 gives r = 3r0 and V = 27(4/3)pi r0^3; A = 216 gives r = 6r0 and V = 216(4/3)pi r0^3, the same volume per nucleon

S03-13.method: scale the length, then square it, then multiply back up by N
S03-13.working: each small cube has side L N^(-1/3), so one piece has area 6 L^2 N^(-2/3).  all N together give 6 L^2 N^(1/3), and dividing by the original 6 L^2 leaves N^(1/3).  check on N = 8: side L/2, eight pieces of area 1.5 L^2 give 12 L^2 against 6 L^2, a factor of 2 = 8^(1/3)

S03-14.method: separate the variables, then integrate the speed
S03-14.working: a = dv/dt = -kv separates to dv/v = -k dt, so v = u e^(-kt). Distance = integral of v dt from 0 to infinity = u/k. Check by dimensions: [u/k] = (m s^-1)/(s^-1) = m, a length. Check the size: a larger k stops the particle sooner, and u/k falls as k rises

S03-15.method: impulse is the area under the force-time graph
S03-15.working: the graph is a triangle of base 0.20 s and height 20 N, so impulse = (1/2) x 0.20 x 20 = 2.0 N s. That is the change in momentum from rest, so v = 2.0/2.0 = 1.0 m/s. Check the size: an average force of 10 N acting for 0.20 s on 2.0 kg gives 10 x 0.20/2.0 = 1.0 m/s

S03-16.method: divide the resolved equations to remove N and m
S03-16.working: resolve: N cos(theta) = mg vertically and N sin(theta) = mv^2/r horizontally. Dividing gives tan(theta) = v^2/(rg) = 15^2/(30 x 10) = 225/300 = 0.75, and tan(37 deg) is about 0.75, so theta is 37 deg. Check the direction: a faster car needs a steeper bank, and 0.75 is just below 1, so the angle is just below 45 deg

S03-17.method: rearrange symbolically: stress sets the area, and the area sets the diameter
S03-17.working: sigma = mg/A so A = mg/sigma.  A = pi d^2/4, so pi d^2/4 = mg/sigma and d^2 = 4mg/(pi sigma), giving d = sqrt(4mg/(pi sigma)).  Numeric spot check with m = 1000, g = 10, sigma = 1.0e9: d^2 = 1.3e-5 m^2 and d = 3.6 mm, which is a sensible cable for a tonne

S03-18.working: d = 1 mm/300 = 3.33e-6 m. The highest order is set by sin(theta) <= 1, so n <= d/lambda = 3.33e-6/5.0e-7 = 6.67 and the largest whole number is 6. Check the next one: n = 7 would need sin(theta) = 7 x 5.0e-7/3.33e-6 = 1.05, which does not exist

S03-19.method: the lens equation, then a separate ratio
S03-19.working: 1/v = 1/f - 1/u = 1/20 - 1/30 = (3 - 2)/60 = 1/60, so v = 60 cm. Magnification m = v/u = 60/30 = 2. Check the region: the object sits between f and 2f, which gives a real image beyond 2f magnified by more than one, and 2 is more than one

S03-20.method: convert the ratings to resistances, then share a common current
S03-20.working: R = V^2/P, so R_60 = 240^2/60 = 960 ohm and R_100 = 240^2/100 = 576 ohm. In series the current is common, so each lamp takes I^2 R and the larger resistance takes the larger share; 960 is greater than 576, so the 60 W lamp is brighter. Check numerically: 960:576 = 5:3, total 1536 ohm, I = 240/1536 = 0.156 A, giving 23 W in the 60 W lamp and 14 W in the 100 W lamp

S03-21.method: series capacitors share the voltage inversely with C
S03-21.working: series capacitors carry the same charge, so V = Q/C makes the voltages inversely proportional to the capacitances: 2.0 and 6.0 uF share 12 V in the ratio 6:2 = 3:1, so the 2.0 uF takes 9.0 V. Check: C_series = (2.0 x 6.0)/8.0 = 1.5 uF, Q = 1.5e-6 x 12 = 1.8e-5 C, and V = Q/C = 1.8e-5/2.0e-6 = 9.0 V

S03-22.working: delta_L = L0 alpha delta_T = 2.0 x 1.9e-5 x (120 - 20) = 2.0 x 1.9e-5 x 100 = 3.8e-3 m = 3.8 mm. Check the size: the fractional change is 1.9e-5 x 100 = 1.9e-3, about two parts in a thousand, and 1.9e-3 x 2.0 m = 3.8 mm

S03-23.method: multiply the mass defect by c squared
S03-23.working: E = delta_m c^2 = 3.6e-30 x (3.0e8)^2 = 3.6e-30 x 9.0e16 = 3.24e-13 J. Check the order: 1e-30 kg is about 0.6 atomic mass units converted wholly, which should be a few hundred keV to a couple of MeV, and 3.24e-13 J is about 2.0 MeV

S03-24.method: photon energy minus the work function, read as volts
S03-24.working: photon energy = 1240/400 = 3.1 eV. Maximum kinetic energy = 3.1 - 2.0 = 1.1 eV, and the stopping potential in volts is numerically the maximum kinetic energy in electronvolts, so 1.1 V. Check the direction: the stopping potential must be less than the photon energy, and it is the difference rather than the sum

S03-25.working: weight = 0.50 x 10 = 5.0 N. Upthrust = rho V g = 1000 x 2.0e-4 x 10 = 2.0 N. Reading = 5.0 - 2.0 = 3.0 N. Check the density: the stone is 0.50/2.0e-4 = 2500 kg/m^3, denser than water, so it sinks and the reading stays positive

S04-01.method: find the internal resistance from the lost volts, then re-divide
S04-01.working: I = 4.8/12 = 0.40 A; lost volts = 6.0 - 4.8 = 1.2 V, so r = 1.2/0.40 = 3.0 ohm. With 6.0 ohm in place: total 9.0 ohm, I = 6.0/9.0 = 2/3 A, V = (2/3) x 6.0 = 4.0 V. Check the direction: the new resistor is smaller so the terminal voltage must fall below 4.8 V, and 4.0 V is below it

S04-02.method: put the dimensions of each option into GM and r
S04-02.working: [G] = N m^2 kg^-2 = (kg m s^-2) m^2 kg^-2 = m^3 kg^-1 s^-2, so [GM] = m^3 s^-2. Then r^3/GM has dimensions m^3/(m^3 s^-2) = s^2 and its square root is s. Check the runner-up: GM/r is m^3 s^-2/m = m^2 s^-2, whose root is m/s, a speed and not a time

S04-03.method: moments about the foot, then divide friction by the normal reaction
S04-03.working: The wall is smooth so it gives only a horizontal R; hence N = W and F = R. Moments about the foot: R x L sin30 = W x (L/2) cos30, so R = W/(2 tan30) = W/(2/sqrt3) = W sqrt3/2. Then mu = F/N = R/W = sqrt3/2. Check the limit: a ladder stood upright needs no friction, and the general expression 1/(2 tan theta) goes to zero as theta goes to 90 degrees

S04-04.method: reduce from the inside out: inner pair, then the branch, then the outer parallel section, then the total
S04-04.working: R4 and R5 in parallel: (12 x 6.0)/(12 + 6.0) = 72/18 = 4.0 ohm. The lower branch is R3 + 4.0 = 8.0 + 4.0 = 12 ohm. In parallel with R2 = 6.0 ohm: (6.0 x 12)/(18) = 4.0 ohm, so the total is 4.0 + 4.0 = 8.0 ohm and the battery current is 12/8.0 = 1.5 A. The parallel section carries all of it and has 1.5 x 4.0 = 6.0 V across it, so the lower branch takes 6.0/12 = 0.50 A and NOT the 0.75 A an equal split would give. Across the inner pair: 0.50 x 4.0 = 2.0 V, so I(R4) = 2.0/12 = 1/6 A. Check by adding the pair: I(R5) = 2.0/6.0 = 1/3 A, and 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/2 A, which is the branch current

S04-05.method: multiply the rate out to a lifetime and read the exponent
S04-05.working: 70 x 60 = 4200 beats an hour; x 24 = 100800 a day; x 365 = 36792000 a year; x 80 = 2943360000, which is 2.9 x 10^9. Check by a second route: a rate of about 10^2 a minute, a year of about 5 x 10^5 minutes and 80 years of about 4 x 10^7 minutes give 10^2 x 4 x 10^7 = 4 x 10^9, the same power of ten

S04-06.method: compare the time of flight at the two angles
S04-06.working: Time of flight is 2u sin(theta)/g, so the ratio is sin60/sin30 = (sqrt3/2)/(1/2) = sqrt3. Check the companion quantities: the 60-degree ball rises three times as high, since sin^2 60 = 3/4 against sin^2 30 = 1/4, but stays up only sqrt3 times as long

S04-07.method: resolve the velocity along and perpendicular to the wall
S04-07.working: The component along the wall, v sin(theta), is unchanged. The component along the normal reverses, from +v cos(theta) to -v cos(theta), a change of 2v cos(theta), so the change in momentum is 2mv cos(theta). Check the limit theta = 0, a head-on bounce: the expression becomes 2mv, which is right

S04-08.method: set gravity equal to the centripetal requirement at the top
S04-08.working: At the top the weight and the normal reaction both point to the centre, so mg + N = mv^2/r. Contact is just lost when N = 0, leaving mg = mv^2/r and v = sqrt(gr). Check the runner-up: sqrt(2gr) is the speed needed to reach the top from the bottom, which is a different question

S04-09.method: the wave speed is the square root of the tension
S04-09.working: v = sqrt(T/mu), so v is proportional to sqrt(T). The tension rises to 121/100 of its old value, whose square root is 11/10, so the new speed is 40 x 11/10 = 44 m/s. Check the fraction: 1.1^2 = 1.21, which is exactly the stated 21 per cent rise

S04-10.method: Snell at the end face, then the critical condition at the wall
S04-10.working: sin i = n sin r at the end face. At the side wall the ray makes an angle 90 - r with the normal, so total internal reflection needs sin(90 - r) >= 1/n, that is cos r >= 1/n. The largest sin i comes from the largest r, at cos r = 1/n, giving sin r = sqrt(1 - 1/n^2) and sin i = n sqrt(1 - 1/n^2) = sqrt(n^2 - 1). Check n = sqrt2: sin i = 1, the grazing limit, which is the largest value possible

S04-11.method: share the supply in the ratio of the two resistances
S04-11.working: The same current passes through both arms, so the output across the fixed resistor is 6.0 x 2.0/(1.0 + 2.0) = 6.0 x 2/3 = 4.0 V. Check the direction: the warm thermistor has fallen to half the fixed resistance, so it takes only a third of the supply and the output must be above half of 6.0 V, as 4.0 V is

S04-12.method: combine the volume and the mass scaling laws
S04-12.working: R = r0 A^(1/3), so V = (4/3)pi R^3 is proportional to (A^(1/3))^3 = A. The mass is proportional to the mass number A. Density is mass over volume, so it goes as A/A, a constant, and the ratio is 1. Check with 8A: the radius doubles, the volume rises by 2^3 = 8 and the mass rises by 8, leaving the density unchanged

S04-13.method: multiply the gradient by the electronic charge
S04-13.working: eV = hf - W rearranges to V = (h/e)f - W/e, so the gradient of the graph is h/e. Then h = e x gradient = 1.6e-19 x 4.0e-15 = 6.4e-34 J s. Check the units: C x V s = (J/V) x V s = J s. Check the size against the accepted 6.6e-34, which it matches to two figures

S04-14.method: solve the equation for eta and reduce to base units
S04-14.working: eta = F/(6 pi r v), and 6 pi is dimensionless. [F] = kg m s^-2, [r] = m and [v] = m s^-1, so [eta] = kg m s^-2 / (m x m s^-1) = kg m s^-2 / (m^2 s^-1) = kg m^-1 s^-1. Check against a familiar value: water has a viscosity of about 1e-3 in these units, and the pascal second is a large viscosity, which fits

S04-15.method: the flight time is proportional to the vertical launch speed, and the horizontal speed is never touched by a bounce
S04-15.working: First fall: 20 = 0.5 x 10 x t^2, so t^2 = 4 and t = 2.0 s, giving a first leg of 15 x 2.0 = 30 m. The vertical speed at the first bounce is 10 x 2.0 = 20 m/s; halved and reversed it is 10 m/s upward, so the second flight lasts 2 x 10/10 = 2.0 s and covers another 15 x 2.0 = 30 m. Halved again to 5.0 m/s the third flight lasts 1.0 s and covers 15 m. Total 30 + 30 + 15 = 75 m. Check: the ball is in the air 2.0 + 2.0 + 1.0 = 5.0 s and 15 x 5.0 = 75 m, and the three flight times are in the ratio 2:2:1, which is exactly the ratio of the vertical speeds 20:10:5

S04-16.method: resolve in two directions and eliminate one tension
S04-16.working: Horizontally T_L sin60 = T_R sin30, so T_L (sqrt3/2) = T_R/2 and T_L = T_R/sqrt3. Vertically T_L cos60 + T_R cos30 = W, so T_R/(2 sqrt3) + T_R sqrt3/2 = W, giving T_R (1 + 3)/(2 sqrt3) = T_R (2/sqrt3) = W and T_R = W sqrt3/2. Check the size: the right-hand wire hangs closer to the vertical, so it carries more than half the weight, and sqrt3/2 = 0.87 is more than a half

S04-17.method: divide the horizontal equation by the vertical one
S04-17.working: The bob moves on a circle of radius r = L sin(theta). Vertically T cos(theta) = mg; horizontally T sin(theta) = m omega^2 r. Dividing gives tan(theta) = omega^2 L sin(theta)/g, so omega^2 = g/(L cos(theta)) and the period is 2 pi sqrt(L cos(theta)/g). Check the limit theta = 0: the expression becomes 2 pi sqrt(L/g), the simple pendulum, which is right

S04-18.method: extension goes inversely with the cross-sectional area
S04-18.working: x = FL/(AE), and F, L and E are the same for both wires, so x is proportional to 1/A and A is proportional to d^2. The second wire has twice the diameter and therefore four times the area, so one quarter of the extension: the ratio is 1/4. Check the direction: a thicker wire is stiffer, so its extension must be the smaller, and 1/4 is smaller

S04-19.method: the two resonances are the first and the third harmonic
S04-19.working: A pipe closed at one end resonates at f, 3f, 5f, so 400 Hz and 1200 Hz are the first and third, and 1200 = 3 x 400 confirms the assignment. The fundamental has wavelength 4L, so L = v/(4f) = 340/(4 x 400) = 340/1600 = 0.2125 m, about 0.21 m. Check the neighbours: 0.85 m would be a quarter of 340/100, a fundamental of 100 Hz rather than 400 Hz

S04-20.method: the critical angle is fixed by the refractive index
S04-20.working: The light starts inside the material, so it emerges only while the angle of incidence stays below the critical angle: sin C = 1/n = 1/sqrt2, so C = 45 degrees. Check the exactness: sin45 = 1/sqrt2 precisely, so 45 degrees is the exact answer and not a rounded value

S04-21.method: reduce the parallel pair, then use the total resistance
S04-21.working: 6.0 || 3.0 = (6.0 x 3.0)/(6.0 + 3.0) = 18/9 = 2.0 ohm; total = 2.0 + 2.0 = 4.0 ohm; I = 6.0/4.0 = 1.5 A. Check the size: with negligible internal resistance the current must exceed 6.0/6.0 = 1.0 A, the value if the battery saw 6.0 ohm, and 1.5 A does

S04-22.method: conserve charge, then divide by the total capacitance
S04-22.working: The charge has nowhere to go, so it is still 48 uC, and the two capacitors end up in parallel, C = 4.0 + 8.0 = 12 uF. Then V = Q/C = 48/12 = 4.0 V. Check the direction: the shared voltage must be below the original 48/4.0 = 12 V, because the same charge now sits on more capacitance, and 4.0 V is below it

S04-23.working: 0.40 c (90 - T) = 0.10 c (T - 10), so 36 - 0.4T = 0.1T - 1 and 37 = 0.5T, giving T = 74 C. Check the position: the masses are in the ratio 4:1, so the final temperature sits one fifth of the way from 90 towards 10, and 90 - 16 = 74

S04-24.working: 24/8.0 = 3 half-lives, so the fraction remaining is (1/2)^3 = 1/8. Check the distractor: 1/3 is what a linear decay would give, but each half-life halves what is left rather than removing a fixed amount

S04-25.method: equal wavelengths mean equal momenta, then kinetic energy goes as 1/m
S04-25.working: lambda = h/p, so equal de Broglie wavelengths mean equal momenta. With KE = p^2/(2m) and p the same, the kinetic energy is inversely proportional to the mass, so KE_electron/KE_proton = m_proton/m_electron = 1836. Check the direction: the lighter particle carries more kinetic energy at the same momentum, and 1836 is more than 1

S05-01.method: build the product of powers and write one equation for each base dimension
S05-01.working: Suppose the answer is rho^a v^b d^c. Its dimensions are M^a L^(-3a+b+c) T^(-b), and the target is M T^-1. Mass: a = 1. Time: -b = -1, so b = 1. Length: -3(1) + 1 + c = 0, so c = 2. The combination is rho v d^2, and substituting back gives M L^-3 x L T^-1 x L^2 = M T^-1, the lengths cancelling exactly. Check the physics: density times speed times area is a volume per second times a density, which is a mass per second

S05-02.working: clockwise: 150 N at 2.0 m plus 45 N at 4.0 m = 300 + 180 = 480 N m. Only the vertical part of the cable tension turns the rod; with a 3-4-5 triangle that part is T x 3/5 acting at 4.0 m, so (3T/5) x 4.0 = 480, 12T/5 = 480, T = 200 N

S05-03.method: the two branch currents give the two midpoint voltages
S05-03.working: left branch total 2.0 + 6.0 = 8.0 ohm, so its top 2.0 ohm drops 12 x 2/8 = 3.0 V; right branch total 6.0 + 3.0 = 9.0 ohm, so its top 6.0 ohm drops 12 x 6/9 = 8.0 V. X sits 3.0 V below the top rail, Y sits 8.0 V below it, so V_X - V_Y = 8.0 - 3.0 = 5.0 V

S05-04.method: multiply out the seconds in a year
S05-04.working: 365 x 24 x 3600 = 31,536,000 s. log10 of that is 7.5 and it is just under 10^7.5, so the nearest power of ten is 10^7

S05-05.method: area under the v-t graph: two triangles plus a rectangle
S05-05.working: triangle 0-5 s = 1/2 x 5 x 20 = 50 m; rectangle 5-15 s = 10 x 20 = 200 m; triangle 15-19 s = 1/2 x 4 x 20 = 40 m; total = 50 + 200 + 40 = 290 m

S05-06.method: three stages: energy on the ramp, work against friction, then momentum through an inelastic collision
S05-06.working: The ramp is smooth, so the kinetic energy at its foot is m g h = 0.50 x 10 x 0.40 = 2.0 J. Friction on the 0.50 kg ball is 0.20 x 0.50 x 10 = 1.0 N, so over 1.0 m it takes 1.0 J and the kinetic energy at the collision is 2.0 - 1.0 = 1.0 J. Hence v = sqrt(2 x 1.0 / 0.50) = 2.0 m/s and p = 0.50 x 2.0 = 1.0 kg m/s. Sticking conserves momentum: V = 1.0 / 0.80 = 1.25 m/s, so the kinetic energy is 0.5 x 0.80 x 1.25^2 = 0.625 J, and the collision destroyed 0.375 J of the 1.0 J. Friction on the combined mass is 0.20 x 0.80 x 10 = 1.6 N, so the distance is 0.625 / 1.6 = 0.3906 m, which is 0.39 m to two significant figures

S05-07.method: energy between lowest and highest points, then taut-string condition at the top
S05-07.working: 1/2 m u^2 = m g (2r) + 1/2 m v^2, so v^2 = u^2 - 4gr. At the top the string stays taut if m v^2/r >= m g, i.e. v^2 >= g r, so u^2 - 4gr >= g r, u^2 >= 5gr, u >= sqrt(5gr)

S05-08.method: transverse velocity is -wave speed times the local slope
S05-08.working: v_y = -v (dy/dx). At Q the slope dy/dx = -0.40, so v_y = -1.5 x (-0.40) = +0.60 m/s, i.e. 0.60 m/s upward

S05-10.method: net emf over the total resistance
S05-10.working: the cells oppose, so net emf = 12 - 6 = 6 V. Total resistance = 3.0 + 1.0 + 2.0 = 6.0 ohm. I = 6 / 6.0 = 1.0 A

S05-11.working: 24 days / 8.0 days = 3 half-lives, so the fraction remaining is (1/2)^3 = 1/8

S05-13.method: average speed, then convert m/s to km/h
S05-13.working: speed = 100 m / 10 s = 10 m/s; multiply by 3.6 gives 36 km/h

S05-14.method: time of fall from the height, then the horizontal range
S05-14.working: t = sqrt(2h/g) = sqrt(2 x 20 / 10) = 2.0 s; range = 12 x 2.0 = 24 m

S05-15.method: Pythagoras for the resultant, then equal and opposite
S05-15.working: resultant of 3 N and 4 N at right angles = sqrt(3^2 + 4^2) = 5 N; the equilibrating force is 5 N opposite to the resultant

S05-16.method: radius of the latitude circle, then centripetal acceleration
S05-16.working: a point at latitude lambda sits R cos(lambda) from the spin axis, so its a = omega^2 R cos(lambda); the equatorial value is omega^2 R, and the ratio is cos(lambda)

S05-17.method: centre of mass by negative mass
S05-17.working: treat the uncut 2a square as mass 4 at (a, a) and the removed a-square as mass 1 at (a/2, 3a/2); remaining mass 3. x_new = (4a - a/2)/3 = 7a/6; the horizontal shift from x = a is 7a/6 - a = a/6

S05-18.method: fringe spacing beta = lambda D / d
S05-18.working: beta = (500 x 10^-9 x 1.5) / (1.0 x 10^-3) = 7.5 x 10^-4 m = 0.75 mm (convert nm and mm to metres first)

S05-19.method: sin of the critical angle is the ratio of the refractive indices

S05-20.method: intersection of the load line with the diode segment
S05-20.working: load line V = 1.0 - 0.1 I_mA; diode line I_mA = 22(V - 0.55)/0.27. Substituting gives I = 22(0.45 - 0.1 I)/0.27, so 0.27 I = 9.9 - 2.2 I, 2.47 I = 9.9, I = 4.0 mA

S05-21.method: network capacitance first, then the charge on the whole chain, then that same charge on the single capacitor
S05-21.working: the 2.0 and 4.0 microfarad capacitors are in parallel, so they add: C_pair = 6.0 uF. That pair is in series with 3.0 uF, so 1/C = 1/6.0 + 1/3.0 = 0.50 per uF, C = 2.0 uF. The supply delivers Q = C V = 2.0 x 12 = 24 uC. A series chain carries one charge, so the 3.0 uF holds all 24 uC and V = 24 / 3.0 = 8.0 V. Check: the pair holds the same 24 uC, so its p.d. is 24/6.0 = 4.0 V, and 8.0 + 4.0 = 12 V, the supply. The bigger capacitance takes the smaller share, as it must

S05-22.method: three stages: warm the ice, melt it, then warm the water; then divide the total by the power
S05-22.working: warming the ice: 0.50 x 2100 x 10 = 10500 J. Melting it, with no temperature change: 0.50 x 3.3 x 10^5 = 165000 J. Warming the water, now with water's own specific heat: 0.50 x 4200 x 20 = 42000 J. Total 10500 + 165000 + 42000 = 217500 J, and at 500 W the time is 217500 / 500 = 435 s. Check: the melting term alone exceeds the other two put together, 165000 against 52500, which is the shape a heating curve should have

S05-23.working: E = (defect in u) x (930 MeV per u) = 0.20 x 930 = 186 MeV

S05-24.method: photoelectric maximum kinetic energy K_max = hf - phi

S05-25.method: Pascal: the force scales with the piston area
S05-25.working: pressure is equal, so F_large / F_small = A_large / A_small = 40 / 2.0 = 20; F_large = 100 x 20 = 2000 N

S06-01.method: parallel the voltmeter with the 8.0 ohm, then divide the supply
S06-01.working: values read off the figure: 12 V cell, 4.0 ohm, 8.0 ohm, voltmeter 24 ohm across the 8.0 ohm; 8.0 || 24 = (8.0 x 24)/(8.0 + 24) = 192/32 = 6.0 ohm; total 4.0 + 6.0 = 10 ohm; I = 12/10 = 1.2 A; the voltmeter reads the p.d. across the pair, 1.2 x 6.0 = 7.2 V

S06-02.method: propagate a small change through a square root
S06-02.working: T = 2 pi sqrt(l/g), so T goes as l^(1/2); a 4.0 % change in l becomes (1/2) x 4.0 % = 2.0 % in T

S06-03.method: resolve on the incline, then ADD friction because the block moves up
S06-03.working: the figure gives a 30 degree incline; W = 2.0 x 10 = 20 N; along the plane 20 sin 30 = 10 N; perpendicular 20 cos 30 = 17.3 N, so N = 17.3 N; f = 0.25 x 17.3 = 4.3 N down the slope; constant speed so F = 10 + 4.3 = 14.3 N, which is 14 N to two significant figures

S06-04.method: reduce inside out, then walk back down the p.d.s

S06-05.method: estimate a rate times a lifetime, then round on the sqrt(10) boundary
S06-05.working: 70 x 60 x 24 x 365 = 3.68e7 beats a year; over 80 years that is 2.94e9; the boundary between 10^9 and 10^10 is sqrt(10) x 10^9 = 3.16e9, and 2.94 is below it, so the answer is 10^9

S06-06.method: area under the velocity-time graph over the whole 12 s
S06-06.working: triangle 0.5 x 4.0 x v = 2v; rectangle 6.0 x v = 6v; triangle 0.5 x 2.0 x v = v; total 9v; 9v/12 = 3v/4

S06-07.method: two conservation laws, then divide to eliminate v
S06-07.working: mu = 2mv cos(th); (1/2)mu^2 = 2 x (1/2)mv^2 so u = sqrt2 v; then sqrt2 v = 2v cos(th) gives cos(th) = sqrt2/2 and th = 45 degrees

S06-08.method: strain, then stress, then force, then mass

S06-09.working: +3.0 cm and -1.0 cm add to +2.0 cm; with A = 3.0 cm that is 2.0/3.0 of A, so 2A/3

S06-10.method: Snell for the index, then v = c/n

S06-11.method: find the current, then the power in the internal resistance
S06-11.working: I = eps/(R + r); the power dissipated inside the cell is I^2 r = eps^2 r/(R + r)^2

S06-12.method: activity times the interval, valid because lambda t is tiny
S06-12.working: lambda t = 1.0e-8 x 60 = 6.0e-7, far below 1, so the number decaying is N lambda t = 4.0e20 x 6.0e-7 = 2.4e14

S06-13.method: carry every conversion, then round on the sqrt(10) boundary
S06-13.working: 12 x 60 = 720 breaths an hour; 720 x 24 = 17 280 a day; 17 280 x 0.50 = 8640 litres; the boundary between 10^3 and 10^4 is sqrt(10) x 10^3 = 3162, and 8640 is above it, so 10^4

S06-14.method: subtract the velocities as vectors, then Pythagoras
S06-14.working: v_P - v_Q = (15 east) - (20 north); the two are perpendicular, so the magnitude is sqrt(15^2 + 20^2) = sqrt(625) = 25 m/s

S06-15.method: two regimes: accelerating while the string is taut, then friction alone
S06-15.working: driving force 2.0 x 10 - 0.20 x 3.0 x 10 = 20 - 6.0 = 14 N over 5.0 kg, so a = 2.8 m/s^2; after 1.0 m, v^2 = 2 x 2.8 x 1.0 = 5.6; then only friction acts, a = -0.20 x 10 = -2.0 m/s^2, so s = 5.6/(2 x 2.0) = 1.4 m

S06-16.working: mu m g = m v^2/r, so v^2 = mu g r and v = sqrt(mu g r)

S06-17.method: linear expansion over the temperature rise

S06-18.method: receding-source Doppler, then expand to first order
S06-18.working: a receding source gives f' = f u/(u + v) = f/(1 + v/u); expanding gives f(1 - v/u) to first order

S06-19.method: apparent depth is the real depth divided by the index
S06-19.working: 3.0/1.5 = 2.0 m, which is less than the real depth, as a pool must look shallower

S06-20.method: combine the pair, take the pair's p.d., then divide by 2.0 ohm

S06-21.method: charge is conserved and energy is not; compare the two energies
S06-21.working: Q = 4.0e-6 x 10 = 4.0e-5 C; energy before = (1/2) x 4.0e-6 x 100 = 2.0e-4 J; after sharing, C = 10e-6 and V = 4.0e-5/10e-6 = 4.0 V, so the energy is (1/2) x 10e-6 x 16 = 8.0e-5 J; the fraction lost is (2.0e-4 - 8.0e-5)/2.0e-4 = 60 %

S06-22.method: the plateau is the melting stage; power times time over the mass

S06-23.method: count the half-lives, then halve that many times

S06-24.method: set the photon energy equal to the work function at threshold
S06-24.working: hc/lambda = phi at threshold, so lambda = hc/phi

S06-25.method: upthrust equals weight, then cancel g
S06-25.working: rho_w x 0.60V x g = m g, so m = 0.60 rho_w V

S07-01.method: solve for the three exponents, one equation per base unit
S07-01.working: [h] = kg m^2 s^-1, [c] = m s^-1, [G] = m^3 kg^-1 s^-2; write h^a c^b G^d. kg: a - d = 0 so a = d. m: 2a + b + 3d = 1, with d = a, so 5a + b = 1. s: -a - b - 2d = 0, with d = a, so -3a - b = 0, i.e. b = -3a. Then 5a - 3a = 1 so a = 1/2, d = 1/2, b = -3/2. Combination h^(1/2) G^(1/2) c^(-3/2) = sqrt(hG/c^3)

S07-02.method: volume of the slab, times the liquid water content, then grams to kilograms

S07-03.method: cube the ratio, to first order in the fractional error
S07-03.working: V goes as r^3, so V_meas/V_true = (1 + 0.010)^3 = 1 + 3(0.010) + ... = 1.030 to first order; the volume is 3.0% too large. Exact check: 1.01^3 = 1.030301

S07-04.method: divide the height by the range and cancel u^2 and g
S07-04.working: H = u^2 sin^2(t)/(2g); R = u^2 sin(2t)/g = 2u^2 sin(t)cos(t)/g; H/R = sin^2(t)/(4 sin(t)cos(t)) = sin(t)/(4cos(t)) = tan(t)/4

S07-05.method: horizontal component unchanged, vertical component from the fall
S07-05.working: v_x = u; v_y^2 = 0 + 2gh so v_y = sqrt(2gh); tan(theta) = v_y/v_x = sqrt(2gh)/u

S07-06.method: conserve momentum, then compare the two kinetic energies

S07-07.method: treat the hole as negative mass and take moments about the disc's centre
S07-07.working: full disc: area 4 pi a^2 at 0. hole: area pi a^2 at +a. remaining area 3 pi a^2; moment = 4 pi a^2(0) - pi a^2(a) = -pi a^3; centroid = -pi a^3/(3 pi a^2) = -a/3, i.e. a/3 from the centre on the side away from the hole

S07-08.method: set the drag equal to the weight
S07-08.working: at terminal speed the resultant is zero, so mg = k v^2 and v = sqrt(mg/k)

S07-09.method: resolve along and perpendicular to the horizontal; the normals are 30 and 60 degrees from it
S07-09.working: the left face is at 60 deg, so its normal is at 30 deg to the horizontal; the right face is at 30 deg, so its normal is at 60 deg. Horizontally: N_L cos30 = N_R cos60, so 0.866 N_L = 0.5 N_R and N_R = 1.732 N_L. Vertically: N_L sin30 + N_R sin60 = W, so 0.5 N_L + 0.866(1.732 N_L) = W, giving 0.5 N_L + 1.5 N_L = 2 N_L = W. So N_L = W/2

S07-10.method: the centre does not accelerate, so only the rim's own acceleration is left
S07-10.working: the centre travels in a straight line at constant speed, so a_centre = 0. The top point is on the rim, at distance r from the centre, with omega = v/r, so its acceleration relative to the centre is omega^2 r = v^2/r towards the centre. Total a = v^2/r

S07-11.method: find the strain that clamping forces on, then multiply by E
S07-11.working: free expansion would be alpha dT L; the rod cannot change length, so the strain imposed is -alpha dT; stress = E x strain = E alpha dT

S07-12.method: P/rho is fixed by the gas law at constant temperature
S07-12.working: for a fixed mass at constant T, PV = const and V = m/rho, so P/rho = const. v = sqrt(gamma P/rho) is therefore unchanged

S07-13.method: decide which side of 512 the unknown lies on from the direction the beat rate moves
S07-13.working: 4 beats/s means the unknown is 516 or 508. Loading the 512 fork lowers its frequency. If the unknown were 516 the gap would widen and the beats would rise; the beats fell to 2, so the gap narrowed, so the unknown is below 512: 512 - 4 = 508

S07-14.method: similar triangles from the eye to the top of the head and to the feet
S07-14.working: each ray meets the mirror at half the height between the eye and the point it came from, so the mirror spans half the total height: 1.70/2 = 0.85 m

S07-15.method: divide the wavelength by the diameter

S07-16.method: kilowatts times hours times days, then pence to pounds
S07-16.working: 2.0 kW x 3 h x 30 = 180 kWh; 180 x 15p = 2700p = 27 pounds

S07-17.method: the e.m.f. stays at one cell's value while the internal resistances halve
S07-17.working: two 1.0 ohm sources in parallel give 0.5 ohm; I = 1.5/(2.0 + 0.5) = 1.5/2.5 = 0.60 A

S07-18.method: balance length is proportional to e.m.f., so use the ratio of the two lengths

S07-19.method: energy supplied by the battery against energy stored on the capacitor
S07-19.working: charge through the battery = CV, so energy supplied = CV^2; stored = (1/2)CV^2; dissipated = CV^2 - (1/2)CV^2 = (1/2)CV^2; fraction = 1/2

S07-20.method: equate the fall in gravitational energy to mc dT and cancel the mass
S07-20.working: mgh = mc dT so dT = gh/c = (10 x 20)/130 = 200/130 = 1.538 K, about 1.5 K

S07-21.method: absolute temperatures, absolute pressures, then back to the gauge
S07-21.working: T1 = 20 + 273 = 293 K, T2 = 50 + 273 = 323 K. Gauge 2.0 atm means absolute 3.0 atm. p2 = 3.0 x 323/293 = 3.307 atm absolute; back on the gauge, 3.307 - 1.0 = 2.307, about 2.3 atm

S07-22.method: subtract the background at both ends, then look for a power of two
S07-22.working: source alone: 840 - 200 = 640 at t = 0, and 240 - 200 = 40 at t = 80 s. 640/40 = 16 = 2^4, so four half-lives in 80 s: 80/4 = 20 s. Check at 20 s: 640/2 + 200 = 520, which is what the curve shows

S07-23.method: binding energy per nucleon times the number of nucleons
S07-23.working: the change per nucleon is 8.5 - 7.6 = 0.9 MeV; every one of the 236 nucleons gains it, so E = 0.9 x 236 = 212.4 MeV, about 210 MeV

S07-24.method: threshold frequency from the graph, then hc/lambda minus the work function
S07-24.working: the line crosses the axis at 5.0e14 Hz, so phi = 6.6e-34 x 5.0e14 = 3.3e-19 J. At 330 nm, E = (6.6e-34 x 3.0e8)/3.3e-7 = 1.98e-25/3.3e-7 = 6.0e-19 J. KE = 6.0e-19 - 3.3e-19 = 2.7e-19 J; in electronvolts 2.7/1.6 = 1.6875, about 1.7 eV

S07-25.method: photon energy, photons per second, then the fraction of a sphere
